title: The district after Storyville closed
summary: Hazel says places with music stayed open until about 1929 and mentions Tom Anderson, Willie Piazza and the Entertainers.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: So what went on in the district after you were in the city, it was supposed to be closed about the time of the First World War.

It was. But it, it, it, it, what happened after that? It was, it was open back there for years after that, but it wasn't as open, you know, as it, as it was written in. It, it, it, it, other words it was, it was on a, it had a few places back there. They had a place called The Entertainers. And then a fella by the name of Lala had a place back there. And Tom Anderson had the Arlington back there. Well there was, there was three or four places. That had music back there. That had music back there. For, for, oh, I guess maybe up until, I guess up until around maybe, uh, 29 or 30. I don't know. I left here, I left here in 27 and, and went to New York. I don't know whether that, it was, it was still back, but they still had a lot, cause Lulu Whitehead house back there, even after it closed. So that, and for years and years afterwards, this, Octoroon, uh, uh, uh, uh, Willie Piazza, she had a place back there where the project is now. For years, yeah, she still had all the, of course it wasn't like, it, it wasn't wide open like it was, it, it, it was more on a sneak and there was a lot of dollar, two dollar places, you know. Yeah. But, uh.
